title: QPS, Storage & Bandwidth Math
summary: The worked-example layer of estimation: turning users and payload sizes into QPS, storage, and bandwidth figures. Practice the standard formulas — QPS from DAU and actions, peak-from-average, storage from item count × size × replication × retention, bandwidth from QPS × payload — plus cache sizing with the 80/20 rule.
keyTakeaways: Read/write QPS ≈ (DAU × actions-per-user-per-day) / 86,400; use ~10^5 for the divisor.
Peak QPS ≈ average QPS × peak factor (~2-3x, more for spiky traffic).
Storage ≈ items × item-size × replication-factor × retention-period; don't forget replication (often 3x) and metadata/indexes.
Bandwidth ≈ QPS × average payload size; separate ingress (write) from egress (read) since read-heavy systems push far more egress.
Cache sizing via the 80/20 rule: caching the hot ~20% of data often serves ~80% of requests, so you can size the cache to the working set, not the whole dataset.
Keep read and write paths separate throughout — a 100:1 read:write ratio means the read side dominates QPS, bandwidth, and cache design.
Multiply by replication for storage AND account for it in write bandwidth (each write may fan out to N replicas).

questions.q: 150 million DAU each make 20 read requests per day. What is the approximate average read QPS?
questions.explain: 150×10^6 × 20 = 3×10^9 reads/day; ÷ 10^5 seconds ≈ 3×10^4 = 30,000 QPS average. You'd then apply a peak factor to size for the busy period.

questions.q: A system does 30,000 average QPS. Using a 3x peak factor, what capacity should you plan for?
questions.explain: Peak QPS = average × peak factor = 30,000 × 3 = 90,000 QPS. Capacity planning targets the peak, not the daily average, or the system tips over during busy hours.

questions.q: You store 500 million records at 2 KB each with a replication factor of 3. Approximately how much raw storage?
questions.explain: 500×10^6 × 2×10^3 bytes = 10^12 bytes = 1 TB of primary data; × replication factor 3 ≈ 3 TB. Forgetting the replication multiplier is a common under-estimate.

questions.q: Which formula best captures long-term storage for a system that retains data for a fixed window?
options: items × item-size, ignoring replication and retention
questions.explain: New items per day × size per item × replication × how many days you keep them gives the standing storage requirement. Ignoring replication and retention (option 1) undercounts; the QPS/DAU forms conflate throughput or users with stored volume.

questions.q: A read-heavy service serves 40,000 QPS with an average response payload of 50 KB. What is the approximate egress bandwidth?
questions.explain: Bandwidth ≈ QPS × payload = 4×10^4 × 5×10^4 bytes = 2×10^9 bytes/s = 2 GB/s of egress. Read-heavy systems are typically egress-dominated, so this is the number that sizes your serving/CDN tier.

questions.q: Under the 80/20 rule for cache sizing, what is the practical takeaway?
options: You must cache 100% of the data to get any hit-rate benefit
Only 20% of requests can ever be cached regardless of data
The cache must be 80% the size of the database
Caching the hot ~20% of data can serve ~80% of requests, so size the cache to the working set
questions.explain: Access is skewed: a small hot subset absorbs most traffic, so a cache sized to that working set captures the bulk of reads cheaply. You don't need to cache the whole dataset, and the hit potential is on the hot 80% of requests, not capped at 20%.

questions.q: Daily reads are 8.6 billion. Rounding a day to ~10^5 seconds, the average read QPS is closest to:
questions.explain: 8.6×10^9 ÷ 10^5 ≈ 8.6×10^4 = 86,000 QPS. The rounded 86,400 ≈ 10^5 divisor keeps this a one-step mental calculation.

questions.q: You want to cache the hot working set of 1 billion objects averaging 1 KB, assuming ~20% are hot. Roughly how much cache memory?
questions.explain: 20% of 10^9 objects = 2×10^8 hot objects × 10^3 bytes = 2×10^11 bytes ≈ 200 GB. That figure tells you how many cache nodes (each with tens of GB of RAM) you need for the working set.

questions.q: Why should you keep read QPS and write QPS as separate numbers throughout the estimate?
options: Because reads and writes always occur at exactly the same rate
Because they drive different design decisions — reads → caches/replicas, writes → sharding/write path — and are often orders of magnitude apart
Because only write QPS affects storage
Because the interviewer only grades the write path
questions.explain: A typical read:write ratio like 100:1 means the read path dominates and needs caching/replicas while the write path drives sharding and durability — collapsing them into one number hides the dominant force. Both paths matter, and reads certainly affect serving/bandwidth even if not primary storage.

questions.q: A write of 1 KB is replicated to 3 nodes and also written to a message queue consumed by 2 downstream services. Roughly how much write-side traffic does one logical write generate?
options: 1 KB — replication and fan-out are free
~5 KB or more — 3x for replicas plus the queue fan-out to consumers
~0.5 KB — writes are compressed in half
questions.explain: One logical write amplifies: ~3 KB across replicas plus the queue write and its delivery to 2 consumers, so real write-side bandwidth is several times the payload. Assuming replication or fan-out is free is exactly the under-estimate this question guards against.

questions.q: You estimate 10 TB of new data per day with 3x replication, retained for 30 days. Approximate standing storage?
questions.explain: 10 TB/day × 3 (replication) × 30 (days) = 900 TB ≈ just under 1 PB. This shows how replication and retention together dominate storage sizing, and why you'd then consider tiering older data to cheaper storage.

questions.q: Your average QPS estimate comes out to 5 million for a service you know runs on a handful of machines. What should you do?
options: Trust the number and design for 5 million QPS
Re-check your assumptions and arithmetic — the figure likely has an order-of-magnitude error
Multiply by a 3x peak factor and move on
Round it up to 10 million to be safe
questions.explain: A result that contradicts a known real-world scale is a signal to hunt for a misplaced power of ten in your inputs or division. Sanity-checking against reality is the whole point of estimation; blindly designing for or inflating a suspicious number compounds the error.

questions.prompt: Estimate the storage and daily egress bandwidth for a photo-sharing service: 100M DAU, each uploads 2 photos/day at 1.5 MB, and each photo is viewed 20 times/day on average. Assume 3x replication for storage.
points: Raw new storage/day: 2×10^8 × 1.5 MB = 3×10^14 bytes ≈ 300 TB/day; × 3 replication ≈ 900 TB/day (note retention would multiply further).
Daily views: 200M photos × 20 = 4×10^9 view-reads/day serving 1.5 MB each.
Egress/day ≈ 4×10^9 × 1.5 MB = 6×10^15 bytes ≈ 6 PB/day; or ~70 GB/s average, higher at peak.
State replication, note read egress dominates, and suggest a CDN for the egress.
questions.answer: Uploads are 100M × 2 = 200M photos/day; at 1.5 MB that's about 300 TB/day of new data, and with 3x replication roughly 900 TB/day before retention. On the read side, 200M photos viewed 20 times is 4 billion view-reads/day at 1.5 MB each, which is about 6 PB/day of egress, or on the order of 70 GB/s averaged and higher at peak. The egress dwarfs everything, so I'd front this with a CDN and object storage rather than serving photos from the origin, and I'd tier or expire cold photos to control the standing storage.

questions.prompt: How do you use the 80/20 rule to size a cache, and what does it save you? Give the reasoning you'd narrate in an interview.
points: Access is skewed — a small hot subset of data serves most requests.
Caching roughly the hot 20% can satisfy roughly 80% of reads.
So you size cache memory to the working set, not the full dataset.
Compute cache size = fraction-hot × item-count × item-size.
Payoff: high hit rate offloads the database and cuts read latency at a fraction of the memory cost of caching everything.
questions.answer: Real access patterns are skewed, so I lean on the 80/20 rule: caching the hot ~20% of objects typically absorbs ~80% of read traffic. That means I size the cache to the working set instead of the whole dataset — for a billion 1 KB objects, ~20% hot is about 200 GB of RAM rather than a terabyte. The payoff is a high hit rate that offloads most reads from the database and cuts tail latency, at a fraction of the memory cost of caching everything, and I'd validate the assumed hotness against real access logs if I had them.
